section1.title: Note-Taking Skills
section1.introduction: Note-taking is a critical academic skill that transforms spoken information into a permanent record for learning and revision. This section provides detailed strategies, techniques, and language tools for effective note-taking.

howTo.title: HOW TO TAKE EFFECTIVE NOTES: A Step-by-Step Guide

actions: Read the assigned material in advance to build background knowledge
Review previous notes to connect new information
Bring necessary materials: notebook, pens, highlighters
Arrive early to choose a seat near the front
Set specific goals: 'Today I will understand the main argument'
steps.example: Before a psychology lecture on memory, read the textbook chapter on memory models and prepare questions like 'How does short-term memory work?'

steps.step: Step 2: Listen Actively During the Lecture
actions: Focus on the introduction to understand the lecture structure
Watch for verbal and non-verbal cues from the lecturer
Identify the main argument and supporting evidence
Pay attention to repetition, tone changes, and pauses
Write down the topic, lecturer name, and date
steps.example: When the lecturer says 'This is important' or 'The key point is...' immediately note that information. Watch for changes in voice volume or writing on the board.

actions: Write main points only - not everything said
Use words and phrases instead of complete sentences
Employ abbreviations and symbols to write faster
Leave space between sections for later additions
Number main points and indent sub-points
Use bullet points, arrows, or diagrams to show relationships
steps.example: Instead of writing 'The professor said that memory is divided into three main types,' write '3 memory types: sensory, short-term, long-term'

steps.step: Step 4: Review and Revise After the Lecture
actions: Review notes within 24 hours while memory is fresh
Fill in missing details while you still remember them
Highlight key concepts and important definitions
Summarize the main points in your own words
Add questions for further clarification
Organize notes into a logical structure
steps.example: After a psychology lecture, add a diagram showing the relationship between sensory, short-term, and long-term memory. Write a one-sentence summary: 'Memory has three main stages.'

abbreviationSystem.title: Note-Taking Abbreviation System
abbreviationSystem.description: Develop a consistent system of abbreviations to increase note-taking speed.

rows: Active reading, i.e., reading with purpose

abbreviationSystem.passage: Developing a personal abbreviation system dramatically increases your note-taking speed. The most effective systems combine standard abbreviations (like 'e.g.' and 'vs.') with symbols you create yourself. Consistency is key: once you decide that → means 'leads to,' always use it that way. In academic settings, common abbreviations include 'w/' for 'with,' 'w/o' for 'without,' and 'info' for 'information.' Mathematics symbols like '=' and '≠' can also represent comparative relationships. The goal is not to create a new language but to save enough time to capture the main ideas without falling behind the lecturer's speaking pace. Remember that your notes must be understandable to you, so personalize your abbreviation system based on what works best for your learning style.

lectureCues.title: Recognizing Lecture Cues
lectureCues.description: Lecturers often provide verbal and non-verbal cues to indicate what information is important.

rows: "This is important", "Remember this", "The key point is"
Write it down clearly, mark with an asterisk (*)
Number these items in your notes
Include the example to understand the concept better
This is the most important information - write it down completely
Repetition usually indicates something you need to know
Adjust to the shift - the emphasized part is important
Watch for gestures that draw attention

lectureCues.passage: Effective note-takers are skilled at recognizing cues from the lecturer. Verbal cues include explicit statements like 'This is important' or implicit ones like repetition. When a lecturer repeats a concept in different words, this is a strong signal that the idea is significant. Non-verbal cues are equally important: writing on the board, changing tone, pausing for emphasis, or using hand gestures all indicate key points. Expert note-takers actively watch for these cues and adjust their note-taking accordingly. For example, when the lecturer pauses after stating a concept, this suggests that the idea deserves special attention. Students who are aware of these cues can write notes that are more complete and better organized, focusing their effort on what really matters rather than trying to record everything the lecturer says.

section2.title: Grammar: Modals and Infinitives for Giving Advice
section2.introduction: Modals are auxiliary verbs that express attitude, possibility, necessity, or obligation. Infinitives are the base form of verbs. This section provides a comprehensive guide to using modals and infinitives for giving advice, with detailed explanations and numerous examples.

grammarOverview.definition: Modals are special verbs that do not change form (no -s, -ed, -ing) and are followed by the base form of the main verb. They express the speaker's attitude toward the action or situation.
grammarOverview.example: You should study. (NOT: You should to study.)

modalComparison.title: Detailed Modal Comparison: Strength and Usage

rows: "You must submit your assignment on time."
Strong advice with warning of consequences
"You had better start studying or you will fail."
Moral obligation or what is right
Advice about what is correct or expected
"You should review your notes after lectures."
"You need to attend all laboratory sessions."
"You are supposed to read before the lecture."
"You could try studying in the library."
"You might want to discuss this with the instructor."

modalUsageGuide.title: MODAL USAGE GUIDE: Detailed Explanation and Examples

should.title: SHOULD: General Recommendation
should.definition: Used to give advice that is generally recommended. It expresses what is best or right to do in most situations.
should.question: Should + subject + base verb?

examples.sentence: Students should attend all lectures to understand the material fully.
examples.explanation: This is a general recommendation for all students.

examples.sentence: You should not procrastinate your assignments.
examples.explanation: This advises against a common mistake.

examples.sentence: Should I take notes on everything the lecturer says?
examples.explanation: This asks for advice on the appropriate action.

should.passage: 'Should' is the most common modal for giving advice in academic contexts. It suggests that the speaker has considered the situation and has concluded that a particular action is the most appropriate. Unlike 'must,' which expresses absolute requirement, 'should' allows for some flexibility. Students might hear 'should' in various contexts: instructors advising on study practices ('Students should review their notes daily'), peers giving advice ('You should join the study group'), and in written guidance ('Reading materials should be read before class'). Understanding this distinction helps students interpret advice correctly. While 'should' represents the ideal action, it acknowledges that there may be exceptions or alternative approaches.

oughtTo.title: OUGHT TO: Moral Obligation and Expectation
oughtTo.definition: Similar to 'should' but slightly more formal and often used when discussing moral obligation, expectations, or what is socially appropriate.
oughtTo.negative: Subject + ought not to + base verb (less common)
oughtTo.question: Ought + subject + to + base verb? (rare in modern English)

examples.sentence: You ought to treat your classmates with respect.
examples.explanation: This expresses a moral expectation in academic settings.

examples.sentence: Students ought to arrive on time for lectures.
examples.explanation: This expresses what is expected and appropriate.

examples.sentence: You ought not to plagiarize your assignments.
examples.explanation: This expresses the expected ethical standard.

oughtTo.passage: 'Ought to' is a formal alternative to 'should' that carries a slightly stronger sense of obligation or moral duty. In academic settings, it is often used to discuss ethical standards, institutional expectations, and professional behavior. For example, a university handbook might state that 'Students ought to maintain academic integrity' to emphasize the moral imperative. Unlike 'should,' which is used in everyday conversation, 'ought to' appears more frequently in formal contexts like academic writing, official policies, and professional guidance. The phrase 'ought to' can also express what is expected due to circumstances, as in 'You ought to understand this by now,' suggesting that the listener has had enough time or instruction to reach a particular level of understanding.

hadBetter.title: HAD BETTER: Urgent Advice with Consequences
hadBetter.definition: Used when the advice is very important and there will be negative consequences if the advice is not followed. It expresses urgency and necessity.
hadBetter.negative: Subject + had better not + base verb
hadBetter.question: Had + subject + better + base verb? (rare)

examples.sentence: You had better start revising for your final exams.
examples.explanation: This is urgent advice because exams are coming soon.

examples.sentence: You had better not miss the submission deadline.
examples.explanation: There will be negative consequences if you submit late.

examples.sentence: We had better arrive early to get good seats.
examples.explanation: This expresses the importance and urgency of arriving early.

hadBetter.passage: 'Had better' is the strongest form of advice, conveying urgency and warning of potential negative outcomes. Students should understand that 'had better' is not just a recommendation but a warning: if you don't follow the advice, you will face consequences. In academic contexts, this might apply to deadlines ('You had better submit your assignment on time'), attendance policies ('You had better attend the mandatory sessions'), or exam preparation ('You had better study the chapters that will be covered'). The negative form, 'had better not,' is used to emphasize what should be avoided, as in 'You had better not plagiarize or you will face serious consequences.' Because of its strength, 'had better' is often used in conversations between people who have a relationship where strong advice is appropriate, such as between advisors and students, or among close peers.

needTo.title: NEED TO: Expressing Necessity
needTo.definition: Used to express that something is necessary or essential. It can function as both a modal and a main verb.
needTo.negative: Subject + do not (don't) need to + base verb
needTo.question: Do/Does + subject + need to + base verb?

examples.sentence: You need to complete all required courses to graduate.
examples.explanation: This expresses a graduation requirement.

examples.sentence: We don't need to attend the optional workshop.
examples.explanation: The workshop is not mandatory.

examples.sentence: Do I need to register for the exam separately?
examples.explanation: This asks if registration is required.

needTo.passage: 'Need to' expresses necessity and is often interchangeable with 'must' but is more common in modern English. While 'must' is often used for rules and laws, 'need to' is frequently used for personal or situational necessity. In academic contexts, 'need to' is used for requirements, prerequisites, and essential actions. For example, 'You need to have completed the prerequisite course before taking this one.' The negative form, 'don't need to,' indicates something is not necessary, as opposed to 'must not,' which is a prohibition. Unlike modals, 'need' can change form for third person singular ('needs to') and can be used in past tense ('needed to'), making it more versatile in academic writing.

infinitives.title: INFINITIVES: Direct Instructions
infinitives.definition: Infinitives are the base form of verbs, often with 'to' but sometimes without. They can give direct, clear advice without using a modal.

examples.sentence: Sit near the front during lectures.
examples.explanation: This is a direct instruction for better visibility and focus.

examples.sentence: Review your notes as soon as possible after the lecture.
examples.explanation: A direct instruction to improve retention.

examples.sentence: Write down the main points only, not everything said.
examples.explanation: A direct instruction for effective note-taking.

examples.sentence: Use abbreviations to increase note-taking speed.
examples.explanation: A direct instruction for efficiency.

infinitives.passage: Infinitives provide direct, clear advice without the need for a modal verb. They are common in instruction manuals, guidelines, and lists of recommendations. The structure is simple: use the base form of the verb to give a direct instruction. In academic contexts, infinitives are often used in handouts, guidelines, and classroom instructions. For example, a professor might say 'Read chapter three before the next class' or 'Complete the assignment by Friday.' Infinitives are particularly effective when giving a series of instructions, as they create a clear, concise list of actions to follow. Unlike modals, which express the speaker's attitude, infinitives simply state what should be done, making them ideal for procedural guidance.

exercise1.title: Fill in the Blanks
exercise1.instructions: Complete each sentence with the most appropriate modal: should, ought to, had better, need to, or an infinitive.

questions.sentence: You ________ complete your registration before the deadline.
questions.explanation: 'Need to' expresses necessity; 'had better' expresses urgency with consequences.

questions.sentence: Students ________ attend all laboratory sessions to pass the course.
questions.explanation: 'Must' or 'need to' express the requirement.

questions.sentence: ________ (Take) notes during lectures to improve retention.
questions.explanation: Infinitive without 'to' gives a direct instruction.

questions.sentence: You ________ not plagiarize or you will face serious consequences.
questions.explanation: 'Had better not' expresses a warning with consequences.

questions.sentence: We ________ submit our assignments by Friday.
questions.explanation: 'Need to' expresses the requirement; 'should' expresses the expected action.

questions.sentence: You ________ review your notes within 24 hours of the lecture.
questions.explanation: 'Should' or 'ought to' gives a general recommendation.

questions.sentence: ________ (Bring) your textbook to class every day.
questions.explanation: Infinitive without 'to' gives a direct instruction.

questions.sentence: Students ________ respect their instructors and classmates.
questions.explanation: 'Ought to' expresses moral obligation; 'should' gives a recommendation.

exercise2.title: Create Your Own Sentences
exercise2.instructions: Write original sentences giving advice on the following topics.

scenarios.modelAnswer: You should create a study schedule. You had better stop procrastinating. You need to prioritize your assignments.
scenarios.explanation: Three different modals showing various levels of advice.

scenarios.scenario: A student wants to improve their grades
scenarios.modelAnswer: You should review your notes daily. You ought to attend all tutorials. You had better start studying earlier for exams.
scenarios.explanation: Three different modals showing various advice approaches.

scenarios.scenario: A student is distracted while studying
scenarios.modelAnswer: Find a quiet place to study. You should turn off your phone. You had better create a distraction-free environment.
scenarios.explanation: Combining infinitives and modals for complete advice.

dialogue.speaker: Aman
dialogue.text: I'm really worried about the final exam next week.

dialogue.speaker: Muna
dialogue.text: You should start reviewing now. You had better not wait until the last minute.

dialogue.speaker: Aman

dialogue.speaker: Muna

dialogues.analysis: This dialogue demonstrates how different modals are used in real conversation: 'should' for general advice, 'had better not' for a warning, 'ought to' for a recommendation, and 'could' for a suggestion.

dialogues.context: A professor giving advice to a student

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.text: You need to improve your note-taking skills. The exams are very detailed.

dialogue.speaker: Professor
dialogue.text: You should focus on main ideas, not every word. You had better review your notes within 24 hours. Also, develop a system of abbreviations.

dialogues.analysis: This dialogue shows formal advice in an academic setting: 'need to' emphasizes necessity, 'should' gives a general recommendation, and 'had better' expresses urgency about an important strategy.

dialogue.speaker: Chaltu
dialogue.text: I can't seem to understand the lecture material.

dialogue.speaker: Tsedey
dialogue.text: Read the chapter before the lecture. You'll understand much more.

dialogue.speaker: Chaltu

dialogue.speaker: Tsedey
dialogue.text: You should sit near the front and turn off your phone. Also, you might want to record the lectures.

dialogues.analysis: This dialogue shows informal peer advice: an infinitive gives a direct instruction, 'should' gives a general recommendation, and 'might want to' offers a gentle suggestion.

The 'had' is always used in 'had better'
"You should submit by 5 PM." (when it's required)

section3.title: Grammar: Present Perfect Tense
section3.introduction: The present perfect tense connects past actions to the present. This comprehensive guide covers formation, uses, contrast with past simple, and common applications in academic writing.

grammarOverview.definition: The present perfect tense describes actions or states that occurred at some time in the past but have relevance to the present moment.
grammarOverview.structure: Subject + have/has + past participle (verb's third form)
grammarOverview.example: I have studied English for five years. (I started studying in the past and am still studying now.)

formation.title: Present Perfect Formation: The Complete Guide

regularVerbs.example: I have worked hard this semester.
They have played football after class.

irregularVerbs.example: I have gone to the library.
You have read this book before.
We have taken notes on the topic.
We have known each other for years.

formation.passage: The formation of the present perfect requires understanding both the auxiliary verb (have/has) and the past participle. The past participle of regular verbs is formed by adding -ed to the base form. Irregular verbs, however, have unique past participle forms that must be memorized. The choice between 'have' and 'has' depends on the subject: 'have' is used with I, you, we, they, and plural nouns; 'has' is used with he, she, it, and singular nouns. Contractions are common in spoken English: 'I've,' 'you've,' 'he's,' 'she's,' 'we've,' 'they've.' The negative form uses 'not' after the auxiliary verb: 'I have not (haven't) finished,' 'She has not (hasn't) started.' Questions invert the subject and auxiliary: 'Have you finished?' 'Has she arrived?'

uses.title: Five Essential Uses of the Present Perfect Tense

use1.name: Action with Present Result
use1.description: An action that happened in the past but has a result or consequence in the present.

examples.sentence: I have lost my keys.
examples.explanation: I lost them in the past, and the result is that I can't open the door now.

examples.sentence: She has broken her leg.
examples.explanation: She broke it in the past, and the result is that she can't walk now.

examples.sentence: They have finished their assignment.
examples.explanation: They finished it, and the result is that they can submit it now.

examples.sentence: We have run out of time.
examples.explanation: We ran out of time, and the result is that we can't finish now.

examples.sentence: He has passed the exam.
examples.explanation: He passed, and the result is that he can move to the next level now.

use1.passage: This use emphasizes the present relevance of a past action. The focus is not on when the action happened but on its impact on the present moment. When students say 'I have finished my essay,' they are not just reporting a past action but indicating that the essay is now ready. Similarly, 'The teacher has posted the grades' means the grades are now available for viewing. This use is common when reporting current information or answering questions about present situations.

use2.name: Action Continuing to the Present
use2.description: Actions that started in the past and are still happening in the present.

examples.sentence: I have lived in Addis for ten years.
examples.explanation: I started living there ten years ago and still live there now.

examples.sentence: She has studied English since 2015.
examples.explanation: She started studying in 2015 and is still studying.

examples.sentence: We have attended all lectures.
examples.explanation: We started attending and are still continuing.

examples.sentence: They have worked at the university for five years.
examples.explanation: They started working there five years ago and still work there.

examples.sentence: He has been a student since September.
examples.explanation: He became a student in September and still is a student.

use2.passage: This use emphasizes the duration of an ongoing action or state. 'Since' is used with a specific point in time (since 2015, since Monday, since I was a child), while 'for' is used with a period of time (for ten years, for three weeks, for a long time). The action is still true in the present and continues into the future. In academic contexts, this use appears frequently: 'I have studied biology for two semesters' (I am still studying it), 'The professor has taught here since 2000' (she continues to teach), 'They have been in the same study group for months' (they are still together).

use3.name: Experience at Some Time
use3.description: Experiences that have happened at some point in the past, with no specific time mentioned.

examples.sentence: I have never been to Lalibela.
examples.explanation: This is an experience I have never had in my life so far.

examples.sentence: Have you ever visited the National Museum?
examples.explanation: This asks about a past experience without asking when.

examples.sentence: She has traveled to many countries.
examples.explanation: This describes an experience in her life.

examples.sentence: We have seen this movie before.
examples.explanation: This describes a previous experience.

examples.sentence: They have never missed a lecture.
examples.explanation: This describes their experience so far.

use3.passage: This use focuses on life experiences rather than specific events. When asking questions like 'Have you ever studied abroad?' the speaker is asking about an experience at any time in the past, not about a specific event on a particular date. If the answer is 'Yes, I studied abroad in 2018,' the speaker switches to past simple because they are now providing the specific time. 'Ever' is used in questions and negative sentences ('Have you ever...?' 'I haven't ever...'), while 'never' is used in affirmative sentences with a negative meaning ('I have never...'). 'Before' is also common: 'I have read this book before.' In academic contexts, this use appears when discussing experiences: 'I have participated in research,' 'She has presented at conferences,' 'They have received various awards.'

use4.name: Recently Completed Action
use4.description: Actions that were completed in the recent past, often with words like 'just,' 'already,' or 'yet.'

examples.sentence: Ujulu has just cooked dinner.
examples.explanation: She finished cooking very recently.

examples.sentence: I have already finished my assignment.
examples.explanation: I finished earlier than expected.

examples.sentence: They have not submitted their project yet.
examples.explanation: They haven't submitted up to now, but are expected to.

examples.sentence: She has just arrived at the university.
examples.explanation: She arrived very recently.

examples.sentence: We have already completed the reading.
examples.explanation: We finished it earlier than necessary.

use4.passage: This use emphasizes the recency of an action or its completion ahead of expectation. 'Just' indicates that the action happened a very short time ago ('I've just finished my exam'). 'Already' indicates that the action happened earlier than expected ('He's already submitted his application'). 'Yet' is used in negative sentences and questions to indicate something that hasn't happened but is expected ('Have you finished yet?' 'I haven't started yet'). In academic contexts, this use is common in everyday conversation: 'I've just handed in my paper,' 'The professor has already graded the exams,' 'The results haven't been posted yet.'

use5.name: Actions with Indefinite Frequency
use5.description: Actions that have happened multiple times or at various times in the past, with no specific dates.
use5.structure: Subject + have/has + past participle + (often/several times/many times)

examples.sentence: I have read this book many times.
examples.explanation: I've read it on multiple occasions.

examples.sentence: She has visited the library several times this week.
examples.explanation: She has made multiple visits this week.

examples.sentence: We have discussed this topic frequently.
examples.explanation: We've had this discussion multiple times.

examples.sentence: They have attended conferences annually.
examples.explanation: Attendance has happened each year.

examples.sentence: He has asked that question before.
examples.explanation: The question has been asked on a previous occasion.

use5.passage: This use describes actions that have occurred multiple times or with some frequency over a period leading to the present. The emphasis is on the repeated nature of the action rather than specific instances. Expressions like 'many times,' 'several times,' 'frequently,' and 'often' are common with this use. For example, 'I have visited the lab many times this month' suggests multiple visits without specifying when each occurred. This is different from 'I visited the lab on Tuesday' (past simple, one specific time). In academic contexts, this use is common when discussing research findings: 'Researchers have studied this topic extensively,' 'The theory has been tested numerous times,' 'Students have raised this concern repeatedly.'

presentPerfectVsPastSimple.title: Present Perfect vs. Past Simple: The Complete Comparison

rows: Action is finished and in the past
Cannot be used with specific past times
ever, never, already, yet, since, for, just
"I have studied here for two years."
"I lost my keys yesterday." (lost then, perhaps found now)
"The university announced new policies last week."

detailedExplanation.title: When to Use Each Tense
detailedExplanation.passage:
The choice between present perfect and past simple depends on how the speaker views the action. Consider the speaker's perspective:

Use Present Perfect when:
1. The time is not important or not mentioned ('I have read this book.')
2. The action has a result in the present ('I have lost my keys.')
3. The action continues to the present ('I have lived here for five years.')
4. You are talking about experiences ('Have you ever been to Lalibela?')
5. You are giving news ('The results have been announced.')

Use Past Simple when:
1. The time is specific and mentioned ('I read this book last year.')
2. The action happened at a specific time ('I went to Lalibela in 2019.')
3. The action is completely finished ('I lived there for five years. [I don't live there now]')
4. You are telling a story with a sequence of events ('I woke up, ate breakfast, and went to class.')
5. You are asked about a specific time ('When did you meet her?')

Understanding this distinction is crucial for academic writing. Research papers often use present perfect to describe previous studies ('Researchers have found that...') and past simple to describe the current study's specific procedures ('The participants were asked to...')

exercise1.title: Complete the Sentences
exercise1.instructions: Use the correct form of the verb (present perfect or past simple) in the following sentences.

questions.sentence: I ________ (study) English for five years. I ________ (start) studying in 2018.
questions.explanation: 'Have studied' describes ongoing study; 'started' is the specific past event.

questions.sentence: She ________ (never, visit) the National Museum, but she ________ (go) to the Science Museum last week.
questions.explanation: 'Has never visited' is an experience; 'went' is a specific past action.

questions.sentence: We ________ (already, complete) our project. We ________ (finish) it yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Have already completed' emphasizes present result; 'finished' is the specific past action.

questions.sentence: They ________ (not, submit) their assignment yet. They ________ (submit) it last week.
questions.explanation: 'Haven't submitted yet' describes current status; 'submitted last week' is a specific past action.

questions.sentence: I ________ (read) this book before. I ________ (read) it in 2019.
questions.explanation: 'Have read before' describes a previous experience; 'read in 2019' is a specific past action.

questions.sentence: The professor ________ (give) us three assignments so far. He ________ (give) the first one in September.
questions.explanation: 'Has given' describes a series so far; 'gave in September' is a specific past action.

exercise2.title: Choose the Correct Tense
exercise2.instructions: Decide whether to use present perfect or past simple based on the context.

questions.sentence: The exams ________ (start) at 9 AM this morning.
questions.explanation: Past simple because 'this morning' is a specific past time.

questions.sentence: The exams ________ (start). We need to be quiet.
questions.explanation: Present perfect because the start has present relevance.

questions.sentence: I ________ (never, see) such a difficult exam before.
questions.explanation: Present perfect describes a life experience up to now.

questions.sentence: I ________ (see) a difficult exam in 2018.
questions.explanation: Past simple because 'in 2018' is a specific past time.

questions.sentence: She ________ (work) at this university since 2010.
questions.explanation: Present perfect because the action continues to the present.

questions.sentence: She ________ (work) at this university from 2010 to 2015.
questions.explanation: Past simple because the time frame is completely in the past.

section4.title: Vocabulary Building
section4.introduction: Building a strong academic vocabulary is essential for university success. This section provides comprehensive vocabulary development strategies, word lists, and practical application exercises.

vocabularyList.title: Core Academic Vocabulary for Study Skills

rows: Temporary; not lasting; staying for a short time

vocabularyStrategies.title: HOW TO BUILD VOCABULARY: Effective Strategies

strategies.description: Learn vocabulary in context by focusing on how words are used in real texts rather than memorizing lists.
steps: When you encounter a new word, read the entire sentence carefully
Try to guess the meaning from the context before looking it up
Read the surrounding sentences for additional clues
Note the part of speech and how the word is used grammatically
Create your own sentence using the word in a similar context
strategies.example: In 'Do not neglect the reading skills you already possess,' 'neglect' likely means 'fail to pay attention to' because it's about skills people have but might not use.

strategies.description: Learn vocabulary in word families to expand your knowledge efficiently.
steps: When you learn a new word, also learn its forms: noun, verb, adjective, adverb
Learn the different prefixes and suffixes that change the meaning
Practice using all forms in different contexts
Create a word family chart for each new word

strategies.description: Learn words that often appear together in natural language.
steps: Note which words commonly appear with new vocabulary
Learn phrases rather than isolated words
Pay attention to collocations in academic writing
Use collocation dictionaries and corpora

strategies.description: Focus on the most commonly used words in academic texts.
steps: Obtain a list of academic word families
Learn the most frequent academic words first
Practice using these words in your writing
Look for these words in your textbooks

strategies.description: Review vocabulary at increasing intervals to move it to long-term memory.
steps: Review new words after 1 day, then after 3 days, then after 1 week
Use flashcards with spaced repetition software (e.g., Anki)
Recycle vocabulary in your writing and speaking
Test yourself regularly on previously learned words
strategies.example: Day 1: Learn 10 new words. Day 2: Review. Day 4: Review again. Day 7: Review. Day 14: Final review.

exercise2.title: Complete the Sentences
exercise2.instructions: Complete the sentences with the correct collocation.

questions.sentence: You should ________ notes during every lecture.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'take notes'.

questions.sentence: Reading helps students ________ a deeper understanding of the material.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'gain understanding'.

questions.sentence: Effective students ________ good study habits from their first semester.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'develop habits'.

questions.sentence: You need to ________ your notes as soon as possible after the lecture.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'review notes'.

questions.sentence: To ________ good grades, you must study consistently.
questions.explanation: The correct collocation is 'get grades'.
